objectives: Derive the SIR ODEs from mass-action assumptions.

slides.title: The SIR model + mass-action mixing
slides.body:
**Compartmental models** divide a population into mutually-exclusive disease states + write equations for the flows between them. The simplest: **SIR**.

• **S** (susceptible): can catch the disease.
• **I** (infected/infectious): currently sick + can transmit.
• **R** (recovered, immune): no longer susceptible (or dead — doesn't matter for transmission dynamics).

Mass-action assumption: each infectious person contacts each susceptible at rate β (combining contact rate + per-contact transmission probability). Then dS/dt = −β S I / N. Recovery: each infected person recovers at rate γ ≡ 1/(mean infectious period). dI/dt = β S I / N − γ I. dR/dt = γ I.

Three parameters: β (transmission rate), γ (recovery rate), N (population). Often re-expressed via **R₀ = β/γ**: the basic reproductive number, the expected number of secondary cases from one infected person in a fully susceptible population.

Known R₀ values: measles 12-18, polio 5-7, smallpox 3-6, COVID-19 (ancestral) 2-3, flu 1-2, Ebola 1-2. Driven by biology (infectivity, latency) + behavior (contact patterns).

slides.title: Herd immunity + the effective R
slides.body:
**Herd-immunity threshold (HIT)**: the fraction of the population needing immunity to prevent sustained transmission. From SIR: each infected person now contacts only S/N susceptibles on average. The **effective R**: R_eff = R₀ × (S/N). Sustained transmission stops when R_eff < 1, i.e., S/N < 1/R₀, i.e., immune fraction ≥ **1 − 1/R₀**.

For measles (R₀ = 15): HIT = 1 − 1/15 ≈ 93%. Hence the public health goal of >95% MMR coverage to prevent outbreaks. Dropping below 93% — even by a few percent — turns measles back from contained to epidemic.

For COVID-19 (R₀ ≈ 2.5 ancestral): HIT ≈ 60%. With Delta (R₀ ≈ 5-6): ~80%. Variants kept raising the bar; combined with waning vaccine-induced immunity, the 'herd immunity goal' kept slipping out of reach.

Caveats: R_eff is not just S-dependent. **Behavior changes** (distancing, masks) reduce β temporarily. **Variant evolution** raises R₀. **Heterogeneous mixing** (some people contact many; most contact few) means HIT in the highly-mixing subgroup matters more than the population average. Real-world HIT often differs from the simple 1 − 1/R₀ formula.

slides.title: Beyond SIR: SEIR, age-structure, networks, stochasticity
slides.body:
Real diseases motivate richer models:

• **SEIR**: adds an **Exposed** (latent, infected but not yet infectious) compartment. Captures incubation period. Relevant when latent period is long compared to infectious period (HIV, TB).
• **Age-structured SIR**: separate compartments per age group with explicit contact matrix (e.g., POLYMOD survey for Europe). Captures the fact that children mix with children, elderly with elderly, mixing only partially across.
• **Network models**: individuals are nodes; transmission only along edges. Captures clustering, super-spreaders, contact-network topology. Helps explain why COVID-19 outbreaks were driven by ~10% of infected (super-spreading events).
• **Stochastic models**: small numbers (early outbreak, extinction) need probabilistic treatment. Branching processes / Gillespie algorithm. The deterministic SIR predicts smooth growth from any infected individual — but a single infected person *might* fail to transmit by chance.
• **Spatial models**: gravity / radiation models for human mobility (commuting, air travel). Used for global pandemic simulations (GLEAM, EpiCast).

Each added complexity buys realism but costs identifiability + tractability. A common modeling principle: start with the simplest model that explains the phenomenon; add complexity only when needed.

question.question: Derive the herd-immunity threshold for measles from R₀ = 15
question.goal: Show why measles needs >93% vaccination coverage + connect to the effective R.

steps.prompt: Define R_eff in terms of R₀ + the susceptible fraction.
steps.motivation: Account for the fact that only susceptibles can be infected.
hints: Each infected meets S/N susceptibles, multiplying by transmission per contact gives R0 × S/N.
steps.reveal: R_eff(t) = R₀ × S(t)/N. As people become immune (recover or vaccinate), S/N falls + R_eff falls.

steps.prompt: What value of S/N makes R_eff = 1 (transmission just barely sustained)?
steps.reveal: S/N = 1/R₀ = 1/15 ≈ 0.0667 = 6.67%. Below this S/N, R_eff < 1 + the disease cannot sustain transmission.

steps.prompt: What's the immune fraction at this threshold?
steps.reveal: Immune fraction = 1 − 1/R₀ = 14/15 ≈ 93.3%. This is the herd-immunity threshold for measles.

steps.prompt: Why does vaccination coverage need to be even higher than the HIT in practice?
hints: Coverage ≠ immunity if vaccine isn't 100% effective.
steps.reveal: MMR efficacy is ~97% (2 doses). So 95% coverage × 97% efficacy = 92% effective immunity — barely above HIT. Also, heterogeneous mixing means that the children-children network can have local R_eff > 1 even when the population average is below HIT. CDC targets >95% coverage to maintain safety margin + handle local pockets of refusal.

steps.prompt: What happens when MMR coverage drops to 88% in a community? Apply your model.
hints: Compute R_eff at this coverage level.
steps.reveal: Effective immunity ≈ 0.88 × 0.97 = 85%. S/N ≈ 15% ⇒ R_eff = 15 × 0.15 ≈ 2.25 — disease can spread. Recent measles outbreaks (e.g., Disneyland 2014, NY 2018-19, Samoa 2019 — 5700 cases + 83 deaths) hit exactly when coverage dropped in pockets to ~80-85% via anti-vaccine misinformation. Mathematics is unforgiving: small drops in coverage produce large outbreaks for highly-transmissible diseases.

question.question: Why did COVID-19 'herd immunity' never materialize as predicted at ~60% (R₀ ≈ 2.5 ancestral)?
options: The original R₀ estimates were wrong; the true R₀ was 0.5.

Variants (Alpha, Delta, Omicron) increased R₀ to 5-10, raising HIT to ~80-90%; vaccine + infection immunity waned over months; heterogeneous mixing meant local R_eff could exceed 1 even when global immunity was high. The simple 1−1/R₀ threshold assumes static R₀ + uniform mixing + permanent immunity — none held.
Herd immunity is a hoax with no real meaning.
question.explanation:
Three reasons the simple HIT formula failed for COVID-19:

(1) **R₀ is not constant**. Each variant raised R₀: ancestral ~2.5 → Alpha 4 → Delta 5-6 → Omicron BA.1 ~8-10. HIT rose from ~60% to ~85-90% — a moving target.

(2) **Immunity wanes**. Antibody titers from vaccination or natural infection drop substantially over 6-12 months. People who 'count' as immune at month 6 may be re-susceptible at month 12. The HIT calculation assumes permanent immunity.

(3) **Heterogeneous mixing**. Even 85% population immunity doesn't prevent outbreaks in subnetworks (schools, workplaces, religious communities) where local coverage is lower. The HIT formula assumes well-mixed populations; real populations have clusters.

Lesson: HIT is a *necessary* but not *sufficient* condition for elimination. It's a useful guidepost, not a guarantee. Endemic equilibrium (smaller but persistent transmission) is more realistic for respiratory viruses with these dynamics.

slides.workedSolution: 1 − 1/R₀ assumes (i) R₀ fixed, (ii) immunity permanent, (iii) homogeneous mixing. COVID violated all three. Variants raised R₀; vaccine-induced + infection-induced immunity waned over months; mixing was clustered. Result: endemic equilibrium with periodic waves, not classical 'herd immunity.'

question.question: A super-spreading event accounts for the majority of secondary cases in many COVID-19 clusters. What model feature captures this?
options: Higher β for the entire population.

Over-dispersion: the *distribution* of secondary cases per infected is skewed (most infect 0-1, a few infect 20+). Captured by negative-binomial models with low dispersion parameter k. SIR's mass-action assumption implies Poisson distribution (mean = variance), inadequate for super-spreading.
question.explanation:
Mass-action SIR implies homogeneous transmission per case — equivalent to Poisson(R) per case. Empirically (Lloyd-Smith+ 2005), real outbreaks show *over-dispersion*: most cases produce 0-1 secondary, a few produce 20+. The shape parameter **k** of the negative-binomial captures this; lower k means more dispersion.

SARS-CoV-1: k ≈ 0.16 (extreme over-dispersion, super-spreaders dominate).
COVID-19: k ≈ 0.1-0.5 depending on setting.
Flu: k ≈ 1-2 (moderate).
Measles: k ≈ 0.5-1 (some over-dispersion).

Implication for control: when k is small, focusing interventions on high-risk events (large gatherings, poor ventilation) is more effective than uniform measures. Contact tracing also works *better* at low k — extinct most chains by interrupting just super-spreaders.

Mass-action SIR misses this entirely. Network models + branching-process formulations are needed for accurate dynamics of low-k diseases. The 'overdispersion principle' underlies why backward contact tracing (find the source of *your* infection, not who you spread to) is so much more efficient than forward tracing for SARS-like diseases.

hints: Is the variance of secondary cases per infected case as small as Poisson?
What's the role of dispersion parameter k?
slides.workedSolution: Mass-action gives Poisson-distributed secondary cases. Reality has heavy tails — most infected produce 0-1 secondary, a few 20+. Modeled with negative-binomial; dispersion k captures over-dispersion. COVID's k ≈ 0.1-0.5 means super-spreading is structural. Implications: focus on settings + behaviors that drive outliers, use backward tracing, accept that average R doesn't capture full dynamics.

question.question: A disease has R₀ = 4. What's the herd-immunity threshold as a fraction of the population?

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain the SIR model + R₀ to a curious public-health policymaker. What can policy levers actually change, and how do they map to model parameters?
question.rubric: Mentions: S/I/R compartments + flows; β = transmission rate, γ = recovery rate, R₀ = β/γ. Policy levers map to parameters: vaccination + natural immunity reduce S (move S→R); social distancing + masks + ventilation reduce β; testing + isolation + paid sick leave shorten infectious time → raises γ; antivirals shorten infectiousness or reduce severity. Note that R_eff = R₀ × S/N is what governs the epidemic's trajectory in real time. HIT = 1−1/R₀ is necessary but not sufficient — variants, waning immunity, heterogeneous mixing complicate the simple picture. Real outbreaks need over-dispersion + network models for super-spreading-dominated diseases (COVID, SARS).
